accent_instruction: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent]

pages.name: the speech
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] You've heard the speech. Times are tough. Tighten your belts. Cut spending, push up interest rates, hold wages down. Sounds like common sense... But austerity has a birthday. Economist Clara E. /məˈteɪi/ dug through the archives and found it, right after the First World War. And she argues it was never really about budgets. It was about stopping something.

pages.name: the war
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Picture Britain in 1915. The war is burning through shells faster than factories can make them. And the government doesn't run out of money... It runs out of shells. So it takes charge: what factories make, what things cost, what workers are paid. Italy does the same. And people notice. If the economy can be organised for war... why not for what people need, instead of just for profit?

pages.name: Britain after the war
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] When the war ends, workers don't want to go back. In Britain, union membership doubles, to eight million. In Glasgow, sixty thousand people pack a square, demanding a shorter working week. The government sends in troops... And tanks. Coal miners demand public ownership of the mines. A royal commission backs them. The government ignores it.

pages.name: Italy
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] In Italy, it goes further. In 1919, more than a million workers go on strike. In 1920, half a million take over their factories.
